query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings, the wear performance is governed by the dynamic formation and stability of a continuous, thin oxide (or glaze) layer that is promoted by a refined (fine‐grained) microstructure. The increased grain boundary density in a fine-grained coating acts as abundant nucleation sites for rapid tribo-oxidation and also mechanically stabilizes the growing oxide, resulting in lower friction and improved wear resistance compared to a coarse-grained coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy protective coating with a conventional (coarse-grained) microstructure applied on a substrate.
generation.intervention: Modify the processing (e.g., apply rapid solidification or thermal/laser processing parameters) to produce a fine-grained microstructure in the HEA coating while keeping the overall composition constant.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in an oxidizing (ambient air) environment at a range of loads and sliding speeds that produce sufficient frictional heating, such that tribo-oxidation is activated; applicable over room temperature up to moderately elevated temperatures (e.g., up to ~400 °C) where oxidation is active.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a continuous, thin oxide (glaze) layer at the friction interface, mediated by an increased density of grain boundaries in a fine-grained microstructure.
generation.mechanism: In a fine-grained HEA coating, the larger grain boundary area promotes faster nucleation and repair of oxide debris during sliding, forming a continuous protective glaze layer that lowers the local shear strength and resists delamination. In contrast, a coarse-grained coating produces a more discontinuous and cracked oxide layer that cannot sustain the mechanical demands of sliding, resulting in higher friction and accelerated wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical sliding conditions in air, the fine-grained HEA coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced specific wear rate, along with microscopic observations (e.g., via SEM/EDS) of a more homogeneous and continuous oxide layer, compared to the coarse-grained coating.
generation.baseline: A conventional coarse-grained HEA protective coating produced without additional grain refinement treatments.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEA protective coatings operating in oxidizing environments and under sliding conditions where frictional heating triggers tribo-oxidation (from low load/low speed to higher load/higher speed regimes) and for alloy compositions where oxide formation is thermodynamically feasible. It may not apply to conditions where oxidation is completely suppressed (e.g., in ultra-high vacuum) or when extrinsic lubricants dominate wear behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While separate studies (e.g., PMC9960858 and PMC10241162) indicate that fine grain sizes improve wear resistance through more stable oxide layers and that heterogeneous tribo-layers help protect against deformation, combining these observations into a universal oxide-mediated wear protection mechanism for HEA coatings has not been directly established. The quantitative relationship between grain size, oxide layer nucleation rate, and mechanical stability remains to be demonstrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings with identical compositions but different grain sizes (one set processed to be fine-grained and the other left coarse-grained). Subject both sets to controlled sliding wear tests under identical ambient conditions (fixed load, sliding speed, and distance). Use SEM/EDS to examine the nature (continuity, thickness, and integrity) of the oxide (glaze) layer and measure friction coefficients and specific wear rates.
measurements: Grain size and grain boundary density (via electron microscopy)
Specific wear rate from mass loss or wear track analysis
Continuity and morphology of the oxide layer (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained HEA coatings do not demonstrate a lower friction coefficient, reduced wear rate, and exhibit a less continuous or mechanically robust oxide (glaze) layer compared to the coarse-grained coatings, then the hypothesis—that grain refinement promotes a beneficial, protective oxide layer governing wear performance—would be falsified.

Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.
